## The Politics of Purity: Democratic transformations in Nepal’s southern borderland

Kristen Zipperer

## AUTHOR'S NOTE

Discipline: Anthropology Institution: Harvard University Defence date: 10 December 2025 Supervisors: Ajantha Subramanian, Malavika Reddy, Ieva Jusionyte, David Gellner

1 The Politics of Purity considers how democracy is experienced and morally inhabited in

Nepal’s southern borderland. Based on two years of fieldwork in Birgunj, an iconic border city that has a history of ethnic activism, the dissertation analyses political life in the years following the country’s 2008 transformation from a Hindu kingdom to a federal democratic republic. This transformation is part of a larger phenomenon that scholars have called the ‘democratisation of democracy’ in South Asia, a process in which  groups  historically  marginalised  within  democratic  politics  have  mobilised support to assert their presence and claim formal power. The dissertation considers why, in the years after 2008, there has been growing nostalgia for the monarchy in the city. Drawing on ethnographic research as well as archival materials, the chapters analyse political life in Nepal over the longue durée. They illustrate the ways older social and political forms of space, community, legitimacy and rule have inflected newer political  formations  and  dynamics,  shaping  how  democracy,  political  belonging, accountability and nationalism are imagined and practised in Nepal today. In doing so, the  dissertation  contends  that  historical  orders  and  imaginaries  have  ongoing resonance  in  contemporary  political  life  even  though  they  are  changed  through processes of modernisation and democratisation. Nostalgia for the monarchy should not be seen as an anti-modern desire to return to a lost past but instead as a local vision

for a kind of democratic politics that is grounded in what the monarchy has historically symbolised, including order, social unity and national sovereignty. By foregrounding the importance of local idioms within democratic politics, The Politics of Purity is an argument for taking older historical forms seriously as enduring elements of political life. It challenges dominant narratives that treat non-liberal political imaginaries as indicating an incomplete or failed modernity, and it demonstrates that kingship and democracy do not necessarily operate as antithetical forms in Nepal but as overlapping frameworks  through  which  contemporary  ideas  of  sovereignty,  legitimacy  and accountability are negotiated.

## AUTHOR

KRISTEN ZIPPERER

Kristen Zipperer is an anthropologist and documentary film-maker whose research focuses on

democracy, political transformation and public life in Nepal. She completed her PhD from

Harvard University in 2026 and is currently an independent researcher.
